concept.name: TLS Certificate Lifecycle

relationships.description: Connects TLS Certificate Lifecycle to api gateway in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: The TLS certificate lifecycle governs generating key pairs, proving domain/workload identity via ACME or an internal CA, deploying X.509 certificates without dropping connections, and rotating or revoking them before expiry.
spark.keyTakeaway: Automate issuance and rotation at 2/3 lifetime (e.g., day 60 of a 90-day cert) using ACME or SPIFFE/cert-manager, and reload proxies without restart—manual calendar reminders inevitably cause outages.

concept.whyItMatters: An expired or mischained TLS certificate instantly breaks every HTTPS client, mobile app, and microservice mTLS call with zero graceful degradation. As public CAs move from 398-day maximum lifetimes toward 90-day and 47-day industry mandates (Apple/Google CA/B Forum proposals) and service meshes rotate mTLS SVIDs every 1–24 hours, manual CSR generation and NGINX restarts are operationally impossible.
whenToUse: Securing public ingress endpoints (API gateways, CDNs, load balancers) with automated Domain Validated (DV) certificates via ACME (RFC 8555) and Let's Encrypt or ZeroSSL.
Enforcing zero-trust mutual TLS (mTLS) between Kubernetes microservices using short-lived X.509 SPIFFE Verifiable Identity Documents (SVIDs) rotated hourly by SPIRE or Istio.
Responding to a private key compromise or CA incident by revoking compromised certs and forcing immediate emergency rotation across edge proxies.
whenNotToUse: Hardcoding long-lived (5–10 year) static certificates inside mobile binaries or IoT firmware for certificate pinning—if a CA rotates or a key leaks, devices brick until an app/firmware update.

Terminating TLS inside a single pod when an L7 ingress (Envoy/ALB) already handles public TLS and an internal mesh (Cilium/Istio) manages pod-to-pod mTLS, unless end-to-end app-level encryption is legally required.
keyPoints: A leaf X.509v3 certificate binds a public key (ECDSA P-256 or RSA-2048) to Subject Alternative Names (SANs) and `notBefore`/`notAfter` timestamps, signed by an Intermediate CA.
ACME (RFC 8555) automates issuance via `HTTP-01` (port 80 `/.well-known/acme-challenge/`), `DNS-01` (TXT record `_acme-challenge`—required for wildcard `*.example.com` certs), or `TLS-ALPN-01`.
Always renew at ~2/3 of certificate lifetime (e.g., 30 days remaining on a 90-day cert) so a failed ACME challenge leaves a 30-day buffer for alerting and retries.
Certificate Revocation Lists (CRLs) and OCSP often fail-open in browsers due to latency/privacy; short-lived certs (hours to 47 days) and OCSP stapling (RFC 6066) are far more reliable.
Zero-downtime rotation requires hot-reloading certificates in memory (Envoy SDS, NGINX `nginx -s reload`, Go `GetCertificate` callback) without severing active HTTP/2 or WebSocket streams.

examples.title: Wildcard Kubernetes Ingress Rotation via cert-manager & DNS-01
examples.scenario: A SaaS platform hosts 400 customer subdomains under `*.app.acme.io` behind an AWS NLB + Envoy/NGINX Ingress and needs automated TLS without opening port 80.
examples.outcome: `cert-manager` uses an ACME `ClusterIssuer` with AWS Route53 IAM permissions to create `_acme-challenge.app.acme.io` TXT records every 60 days, stores the ECDSA P-256 leaf + intermediate chain in a Kubernetes `Secret`, and Envoy picks it up via SDS in <2 seconds with zero dropped connections.

examples.title: Hourly mTLS SVID Rotation in a Payment Service Mesh
examples.scenario: PCI-DSS segmentation requires mutual TLS between `checkout-svc` and `ledger-svc` with cryptographic identity tied to Kubernetes ServiceAccounts rather than IP addresses.
examples.outcome: SPIRE Agent issues 1-hour X.509 SVIDs (`spiffe://prod.acme.io/ns/payments/sa/ledger`) over a local Unix domain socket (Workload API); keys never touch disk, and a compromised pod's identity expires automatically within 60 minutes without needing CRL distribution.

tradeOffs.pro: `HTTP-01` requires zero DNS API credentials and works immediately for single-domain public endpoints.
tradeOffs.con: `HTTP-01` cannot issue wildcard (`*.domain.com`) certs and fails for internal/firewalled services; `DNS-01` handles both but requires scoped DNS write permissions.

tradeOffs.pro: ECDSA P-256 keys are ~10x smaller (256-bit vs 2048-bit), cut TLS 1.3 handshake CPU by ~3–5x, and reduce certificate chain bytes on mobile.
tradeOffs.con: Legacy clients (pre-2014 Java 7/Android 4, old embedded scanners) may lack ECDSA cipher support, requiring dual-cert RSA fallback.

tradeOffs.pro: Short-lived certs eliminate revocation infrastructure complexity because compromised keys age out automatically.
tradeOffs.con: Tightens dependency on the local CA/ACME control plane—if the CA is down longer than the TTL, the entire fleet expires simultaneously.

failureModes.name: Missing Intermediate CA in `fullchain.pem`
failureModes.description: Server serves only the leaf certificate instead of `leaf + intermediate`. Desktop browsers (which cache intermediates) pass, while `curl`, Go, and Java clients fail with `unable to verify the first certificate`.
failureModes.mitigation: Always bundle leaf + intermediate(s) in `fullchain.pem` (never include the Root CA) and validate chains in CI with `openssl s_client -verify_return_error`.

failureModes.name: Let's Encrypt Rate Limit Exhaustion
failureModes.description: A broken Kubernetes loop repeatedly deletes and recreates `Secret` objects, hitting Let's Encrypt's 50 certs/week per registered domain or 5 duplicate certs/week limit and blocking valid renewals.
failureModes.mitigation: Test all automation against Let's Encrypt's Staging CA first, persist ACME account keys and issued secrets, and alert on `certmanager_certificate_ready_status == 0`.

failureModes.name: Clock Skew Triggering Premature Expiry / NotYetValid
failureModes.description: A VM or container with NTP drift 10 minutes behind CA time rejects a freshly minted mTLS cert because `now < notBefore`.
failureModes.mitigation: Enforce `chrony`/NTP sync across all nodes and configure internal CAs to backdate `notBefore` by 2–5 minutes.

failureModes.name: Silent Hot-Reload Failure
failureModes.description: cert-manager renews the `tls.crt` file on disk, but the Java or Go microservice loaded the `KeyStore` once at startup and serves the expired cert 30 days later.
failureModes.mitigation: Terminate TLS at Envoy/NGINX with SDS or `fsnotify` reloaders, or use Go's `tls.Config.GetCertificate` / Spring Boot SSL bundles with `reload-on-update: true`.

commonMistakes: Monitoring certificate expiry with a calendar invite instead of Prometheus `probe_ssl_earliest_cert_expiry` alerts at 21 days and 7 days.
Renewing at 95% lifetime (e.g., day 85 of 90) instead of 66% (day 60), leaving too little time to recover from a DNS or CA outage.
Including the Root CA inside the server's TLS certificate chain, wasting ~1.5 KB per TLS 1.3 handshake.
Pinning leaf public keys in mobile apps instead of pinning the Root/Backup CA or relying on Certificate Transparency.
Storing private keys in Git or unencrypted S3 buckets instead of KMS, Vault PKI, or Kubernetes Secrets encrypted at rest.

sections.content:
## The idea

A TLS certificate (X.509v3) is a time-bounded cryptographic attestation signed by a trusted Certificate Authority (CA) binding a domain or workload identity (SAN) to a public key. Because private keys can leak and algorithms age, **every certificate has an expiry**.

Managing TLS at scale means treating certificates as **ephemeral, automated state machines** rather than static config files: generate a fresh key pair locally (the private key never leaves the host/cluster), prove control over the identity (ACME or SPIFFE), install the signed chain, hot-reload the listener, and trigger the next renewal at 2/3 of the certificate's lifetime.

## Concrete walkthrough

Trace an automated 90-day public TLS renewal using **cert-manager** and **Let's Encrypt (ACME RFC 8555)** with `DNS-01`:

1. **Trigger (Day 60)**: `cert-manager` inspects `tls.crt` (`notAfter - notBefore = 90d`) and sees `<= 30d` remaining (`renewBefore: 720h`). It generates a fresh ECDSA P-256 private key in memory.
2. **Order & Challenge**: `cert-manager` submits an ACME Order for `*.api.example.com` to `acme-v02.api.letsencrypt.org` and receives a `DNS-01` token.
3. **Proof of Control**: It computes `base64url(sha256(token + "." + accountKeyThumbprint))` and writes a TXT record `_acme-challenge.api.example.com` via Route53 API, polling authoritative DNS until propagated.
4. **Issuance & CT Logging**: Let's Encrypt validates the TXT record from multiple vantage points, appends the cert to public Certificate Transparency (CT) logs (RFC 6962), and returns `fullchain.pem` (Leaf + Intermediate R10/E5).
5. **Zero-Downtime Swap**: `cert-manager` atomically updates the Kubernetes `Secret`; Envoy (via SDS) swaps the TLS context in memory within ~1 second while existing TCP/HTTP2 streams finish cleanly.

sections.content:
## Revocation, OCSP Stapling & Short-Lived Certs

When a private key leaks, CAs publish a **CRL** (Certificate Revocation List) or serve **OCSP** (Online Certificate Status Protocol) responses. In practice, live OCSP lookups from clients add 50–200 ms to handshakes, leak browsing metadata to the CA, and fail-open when the CA's OCSP responder hiccups.

Two patterns solve this:
- **OCSP Stapling (RFC 6066)**: The *server* (NGINX/Envoy) periodically fetches the CA-signed OCSP response and staples it directly into the TLS `Certificate` handshake message—zero extra client round-trips.
- **Short-Lived Certificates**: Let's Encrypt ended OCSP support in favor of CRLs + short lifetimes (moving toward 6-day optional / 47-day max certs), and internal meshes like SPIFFE/Vault PKI issue 1–24 hour certs so compromised credentials expire before a CRL even propagates.

## ACME Challenge & PKI Strategy Comparison

| Mechanism | Port / Infra Required | Wildcard Support (`*.`) | Works on Private / Firewalled Hosts? | Typical Rotation Cadence |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **ACME `HTTP-01`** | TCP 80 reachable publicly | No | No | Every 60 days (90d cert) |
| **ACME `DNS-01`** | Scoped DNS API token | **Yes** | **Yes** | Every 60 days (90d cert) |
| **ACME `TLS-ALPN-01`** | TCP 443 (`acme-tls/1` ALPN) | No | No | Every 60 days (90d cert) |
| **Vault PKI / Private CA** | Internal Vault / step-ca API | Yes | **Yes** | 24h – 30d |
| **SPIFFE / SPIRE (mTLS)** | Node agent Unix socket | N/A (SPIFFE URI SAN) | **Yes** | 1h – 4h (auto in-memory) |

## Failure modes

1. **Split-Brain Renewal in Multi-Instance Fleets**: Five stateless instances behind a load balancer all run `HTTP-01` locally; the CA's validation request hits Instance B while Instance A holds the challenge token, causing random 403 failures. Centralize issuance in a single controller (`cert-manager`) or use `DNS-01`.
2. **CAA Record Blocking**: A domain's DNS `CAA` record permits only `digicert.com`, causing Let's Encrypt renewals to fail silently until expiry.
3. **Root Store Expiry**: Older IoT devices or unpatched Docker base images (`alpine:3.12`) lack newer Root CAs (e.g., ISRG Root X2), rejecting valid modern chains.

## Observability & Emergency Rotation

Monitor the *served* certificate on the wire, not just the file on disk:

- **Blackbox Exporter (`probe_ssl_earliest_cert_expiry`)**: Probe every public and internal VIP every 60s. Page at `< 14 days` (catches 60-day renewal failures with 2 weeks to spare) and critical-page at `< 5 days`.
- **Chain & Protocol Audits**: Verify `fullchain.pem` completeness, TLS 1.2/1.3 cipher suites, and CAA records on every deploy.
- **Emergency Rotation Drill**: Practice revoking and force-renewing a staging cert twice a year so you know how long DNS TTLs and CDN edge propagation actually take.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Automate issuance and renewal at **2/3 lifetime** via ACME (`cert-manager`, `caddy`, `certbot`) or SPIRE.
- [ ] Serve `leaf + intermediate` (`fullchain.pem`), never leaf-only and never include the Root CA.
- [ ] Verify listeners hot-reload certs without dropping active TCP/HTTP2 connections.
- [ ] Configure Blackbox TLS probing on live endpoints (alert at `< 21d` warning, `< 7d` page).
- [ ] Add `CAA` DNS records explicitly authorizing your chosen CA(s).
- [ ] Never hardcode leaf cert pins in mobile/IoT clients; use short-lived certs and automated CT monitoring.

interviewProblems.title: TLS Certificate Lifecycle
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on TLS Certificate Lifecycle. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: The TLS certificate lifecycle governs generating key pairs, proving domain/workload identity via ACME or an internal CA, deploying X.509 certificates without dropping connections, and rotating or revoking them before expiry.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: ACME CA applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Envoy / NGINX.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Envoy / NGINX experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Always bundle leaf + intermediate(s) in `fullchain.pem` (never include the Root CA) and validate chains in CI with `openssl s_client -verify_return_error`.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Automate issuance and rotation at 2/3 lifetime (e.g., day 60 of a 90-day cert) using ACME or SPIFFE/cert-manager, and reload proxies without restart—manual calendar reminders inevitably cause outages.
Avoid trap: Monitoring certificate expiry with a calendar invite instead of Prometheus `probe_ssl_earliest_cert_expiry` alerts at 21 days and 7 days.
Avoid trap: Renewing at 95% lifetime (e.g., day 85 of 90) instead of 66% (day 60), leaving too little time to recover from a DNS or CA outage.
When to reach for it: Securing public ingress endpoints (API gateways, CDNs, load balancers) with automated Domain Validated (DV) certificates via ACME (RFC 8555) and Let's Encrypt or ZeroSSL.
When to reach for it: Enforcing zero-trust mutual TLS (mTLS) between Kubernetes microservices using short-lived X.509 SPIFFE Verifiable Identity Documents (SVIDs) rotated hourly by SPIRE or Istio.

putItTogether.title: Putting Tls Certificate Lifecycle Together
putItTogether.summary: Automate issuance and rotation at 2/3 lifetime (e.g., day 60 of a 90-day cert) using ACME or SPIFFE/cert-manager, and reload proxies without restart—manual calendar reminders inevitably cause outages.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Tls Certificate Lifecycle before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: `cert-manager` uses an ACME `ClusterIssuer` with AWS Route53 IAM permissions to create `_acme-challenge.app.acme.io` TXT records every 60 days, stores the ECDSA P-256 leaf + intermediate chain in a Kubernetes `Secret`, and Envoy picks it up via SDS in <2 seconds with zero dropped connections.
